title: The carpenter's peg
hookLine: as a carpenter knocks out a coarse peg with a fine one, replace an unhelpful thought (MN 20)

lines: A ROTTEN PEG IN THE JOINT.
cards: Old timber-frame houses were held together with wooden pegs driven through the joints. When a peg rots or splits, a carpenter can't just yank it out; that would wreck the joint.
So one way is to set a slimmer, harder peg against the end of the old one and tap. The new peg pushes the old one out and takes its place, and the joint is never left empty.

teach.b: This picture came up on day three hundred eighty-five, as the first of five ways with a bad thought. Today, a closer look at the peg itself. MN 20, the Vitakkasanthana.

When unwholesome thoughts, tied to desire, hate or delusion, keep arising while a person attends to some theme, the Buddha says, they should attend instead to another theme, one connected with what is wholesome.

Then those thoughts fade, and the mind settles inwardly, grows still, becomes unified. Just as a skilled carpenter, or his apprentice, might knock out a coarse peg by means of a fine one. Three things stand out.
First: the sutta doesn't say yank the thought out.
It says attend to another theme, so the place isn't left empty.

teach.h: THE PEG MUST FIT THE HOLE.
teach.b: Second: the new peg has to fit the same hole.

The later commentary gives examples: for desire fixed on a person, reflect on the body's unattractive parts; for ill will toward someone, loving-kindness; for confusion, ask someone wise, or examine causes with care.
Third: it's a finer peg. Not a bigger, louder thought.
A quieter, truer one. The Dhammapada puts the craft in a line, in Max Müller's translation: “fletchers bend the arrow; carpenters bend a log of wood; wise people fashion themselves.”
This is fashioning, one small joint at a time.

how: Teachers who use MN 20's first method match an antidote to the kind of thought that arises, for example loving-kindness for ill will, following the commentary's examples.

o: stopping all thought by force of will
writing thoughts down to clear the mind
stilling thoughts by swapping in a finer one

games.q: match the pieces of the peg.
p: a theme tied to the wholesome

s: the method says to empty the mind and leave nothing
it says to attend to another, wholesome theme in its place.
the commentary matches each replacement to the kind of thought
loving-kindness for ill will, for example.
the new peg should be a bigger, coarser one
the sutta's peg is a fine one, knocking out a coarse one.

games.q: a resentful thought about a coworker keeps coming back. by the commentary's examples, which finer peg fits that hole?
games.why: for ill will, loving-kindness: the replacement answers the same need, so it actually fits the hole.

practice: Wait for a thought you'd rather not keep, a grudge, a craving, a worry, and ask what hole it's filling.
Then tap in a finer peg that fits the same hole: for the grudge, wish that person one simple good thing; for the craving, feel the body breathing; for the worry, name one honest next step.

wordCard.voice: Vitakka-santhana, the stilling of thoughts. A coarse thought knocked out by a finer one that fits the same place.

orig.note: Pali vitakka-saṇṭhāna: the stilling or settling of thoughts, the name of MN 20.

carryVoice: Your line: a finer peg. Quieter and truer, fitted to the same place. Day four hundred fifteen.

sources.ref: Majjhima Nikaya 20, Vitakkasanthana Sutta (the first method)
